title: DiveLab
text:
1 Welcome
DiveLab teaches dynamical systems and control engineering through one coherent physical system: a scuba diver underwater.
The book provides the narrative. The notebooks provide the executable laboratory.

title: DiveLab
text:
1.1 Educational scope
DiveLab is an educational resource. It is not a diving manual, decompression planner, or substitute for certified training and approved equipment.

title: Preface
text:
Imagine floating effortlessly beneath the surface of the sea.
Everything appears calm. The water is almost still. Your breathing is slow and regular. A small movement of your lungs gently changes your buoyancy.
To an experienced diver, this feels natural.
To an engineer, it is extraordinary.
Beneath this apparent simplicity lies a remarkably rich dynamical system.
Every breath closes a feedback loop.
Every ascent and descent is the response of a nonlinear dynamical system.
Every dive is an exercise in control engineering.
DiveLab began with a simple question:

What if an entire control-engineering course could be taught through one coherent physical system?

The diver is our guide.
The true subject is systems thinking.
Welcome.
Let us begin our descent.

title: 2  Pressure and Depth
text:
3 Engineering Question
The intuitive answer is often: at great depth.
That answer is only partly correct.
Absolute pressure continues to increase as a diver descends, but the largest relative change occurs immediately below the surface. This distinction between absolute change and relative change is the key to understanding why the first metres of a dive are so important.
This chapter develops that idea carefully. We begin with physical intuition, derive the hydrostatic-pressure equation, examine its assumptions, and connect it to the broader systems story of DiveLab.

title: 2  Pressure and Depth
text:
9.1 Gauge Pressure
Gauge pressure measures pressure relative to the atmosphere:
\[
P_{\mathrm{gauge}} = P - P_0.
\]
Using Equation 7.2:
\[
P_{\mathrm{gauge}} = \rho gh.
\]
At the surface, \(P_{\mathrm{gauge}} = 0\).

title: 2  Pressure and Depth
text:
9.2 Absolute Pressure
Absolute pressure is measured relative to vacuum:
\[
P_{\mathrm{abs}} = P_0 + \rho gh.
\]
At the surface, \(P_{\mathrm{abs}} = P_0\).
For gas-volume calculations, absolute pressure must be used.






WarningCommon Misconception



Boyle’s law cannot be applied using gauge pressure. A gauge pressure of zero at the surface does not mean that the gas is under zero pressure.

title: 2  Pressure and Depth
text:
12.1 Numerical Example
Using the diving approximation:

from 0 m to 10 m, pressure rises from 1 bar to 2 bar;
from 10 m to 20 m, pressure rises from 2 bar to 3 bar;
from 20 m to 30 m, pressure rises from 3 bar to 4 bar.

The absolute increase is 1 bar each time.
The relative increases are:
\[
\frac{2-1}{1} = 100\%,
\]
\[
\frac{3-2}{2} = 50\%,
\]
\[
\frac{4-3}{3} \approx 33.3\%.
\]
The first 10 metres therefore produce the largest proportional increase.






ImportantEngineering Answer



The first metres of descent are not special because pressure rises faster in an absolute sense. They are special because the same pressure increment represents the largest fraction of the current pressure.

title: 2  Pressure and Depth
text:
14.1 The Fluid Is at Rest
Hydrostatics neglects acceleration and flow effects.

title: 2  Pressure and Depth
text:
14.2 Density Is Constant
Water is only weakly compressible over ordinary recreational-diving depths, so constant density is an excellent approximation.

title: 2  Pressure and Depth
text:
14.3 Gravity Is Constant
Over diving depths, variation in \(g\) is negligible.

title: 2  Pressure and Depth
text:
14.4 The Free-Surface Pressure Is Known
At sea level this is approximately atmospheric pressure. At altitude, \(P_0\) is lower.

title: 2  Pressure and Depth
text:
14.5 Depth Is Measured Vertically
Hydrostatic pressure depends on vertical depth below the free surface, not on path length travelled.






TipModelling Principle



A model is useful when its assumptions match the question being asked. The simple hydrostatic model is extremely accurate for introductory diving calculations.

18.3 Relative Pressure Change from 5 m to 10 m
At 5 m, \(P_1\approx1.5\ \mathrm{bar}\).
At 10 m, \(P_2\approx2.0\ \mathrm{bar}\).

\[
\frac{P_2-P_1}{P_1}

At 25 m, \(P_1\approx3.5\ \mathrm{bar}\).
At 30 m, \(P_2\approx4.0\ \mathrm{bar}\).
Therefore:
\[
\frac{0.5}{3.5}
\approx
14.3\%.
\]

title: 2  Pressure and Depth
text:
19.1 “Pressure increases faster near the surface”
Not in the constant-density hydrostatic model. The absolute gradient \(dP/dh=\rho g\) is constant. What decreases with depth is the fractional gradient.

title: 2  Pressure and Depth
text:
19.2 “Pressure is zero at the surface”
Gauge pressure is zero at the surface. Absolute pressure is approximately 1 bar.

title: 2  Pressure and Depth
text:
19.3 “Depth travelled determines pressure”
Only vertical depth below the free surface matters.

title: 2  Pressure and Depth
section: 19.4 “A 1 bar increase always has the same effect”
text:
19.4 “A 1 bar increase always has the same effect”
It has the same absolute magnitude, but not the same relative magnitude.

title: 3  Compressible Gases
text:
4 Engineering Question
At first sight, the answer appears obvious.
The diver is surrounded by water, and water is essentially incompressible. If the amount of water does not change, why should buoyancy change?
The answer lies elsewhere.
The most important component of the underwater environment is not the water itself, but the gas trapped inside the diver’s equipment and lungs.
Unlike water, gases are highly compressible.
As pressure changes with depth, gas volume changes accordingly.
Those changes in volume alter buoyancy, and buoyancy alters motion.
This chapter explores one of the most elegant relationships in classical physics:
In this chapter we focus only on the first half of that chain:
Pressure → Volume
The second half,
Volume → Buoyant Force,
will be developed in the following chapter through Archimedes’ Principle.

title: 3  Compressible Gases
text:
11.1 A Fundamental Experimental Observation
Imagine a transparent syringe whose nozzle has been sealed.
Inside the syringe there is only air.
Initially, the piston can move freely.
As we push the piston inward, something interesting happens.
The force required to continue compressing the air becomes progressively larger.
The air resists compression.
If we release the piston, the air expands again, returning almost to its original volume.
Nothing has been added to the syringe.
Nothing has been removed.
Only two quantities have changed:

the pressure inside the syringe;
the volume occupied by the air.

This simple experiment reveals one of the most important properties of gases:

Increasing pressure decreases volume.

The relationship is not arbitrary.
It follows a remarkably simple mathematical law discovered by Robert Boyle.

title: 3  Compressible Gases
text:
11.2 Boyle’s Law
For a fixed amount of gas maintained at constant temperature,
the product of pressure and volume remains constant.
Mathematically,
\[
PV = \text{constant}.
\]
Equivalently, comparing two different states of the same gas,
\[
P_1V_1=P_2V_2.
\]
This equation is known as Boyle’s Law.
Although deceptively simple, it explains nearly every phenomenon involving trapped gas during a recreational dive.






ImportantDiveLab Insight



Boyle’s Law does not describe the behaviour of water.
It describes the behaviour of gases.
Whenever a diver breathes, inflates a buoyancy compensator, observes bubbles, or carries an air space underwater, Boyle’s Law is at work.

title: 3  Compressible Gases
section: 11.3 Where Does Boyle’s Law Come From?
text:
11.3 Where Does Boyle’s Law Come From?
Boyle originally discovered the relationship experimentally.
Today we can derive it from the Ideal Gas Law,
\[
PV=nRT,
\]
where

(P) is the absolute pressure;
(V) is the gas volume;
(n) is the number of moles of gas;
(R) is the universal gas constant;
(T) is the absolute temperature.

During a typical diving manoeuvre, we assume that

the amount of gas remains constant;
the temperature changes only slightly.

Under these assumptions,
(n), (R), and (T) may all be considered constant.
Therefore,
\[
PV=\text{constant},
\]
which is precisely Boyle’s Law.
This derivation also reveals the assumptions behind the model.
Boyle’s Law is not a universal law valid under every circumstance.
It is an excellent approximation for many recreational diving situations.

title: 3  Compressible Gases
text:
11.4 An Inverse Relationship
Boyle’s Law tells us that pressure and volume vary in opposite directions.
If pressure doubles,
volume becomes half as large.
If pressure triples,
volume becomes one third of its original value.
More generally,
\[
V=\frac{K}{P},
\]
where (K) is a constant.
The relationship is therefore inverse, not linear.
This distinction is extremely important.
Pressure increases almost linearly with depth.
Volume does not.
Consequently, equal changes in depth do not produce equal changes in volume.
That observation will become one of the key ideas of this chapter.

title: 3  Compressible Gases
text:
11.5 Engineering Perspective
Control engineers often ask two questions.

What is the input?

In this chapter,
the input is pressure.

What is the output?

The output is gas volume.
The system therefore transforms
\[
\text{Pressure}
\longrightarrow
\text{Volume}.
\]
In later chapters,
this volume will generate buoyancy,
and buoyancy will generate motion.
Each chapter adds one new link to the chain.
The complete diver will eventually emerge as an interconnected dynamical system.

title: 3  Compressible Gases
text:
11.6 Looking Ahead
Boyle’s Law tells us how pressure changes volume.
The next question is equally important.
How much does pressure actually increase underwater?
To answer that question we must distinguish between

atmospheric pressure,
hydrostatic pressure,
and absolute pressure.

Only absolute pressure can be used in Boyle’s Law.
The next section explains why.
